Astrox: Hostile Space Excavation is a quirky little affair. Graphically, a mixed bag. The asteroids are flat, shaded affairs. But still, it's the gameplay that counts and Astrox:Hostile Space Excavation is pretty solid on that count.

Astrox has a nearly non-existent plot line, and very little depth.  Your character is a convict laborer in a space prison, which is somehow overrun with 100 pirate ships for every prisoner mining vessel. When reaching the final level, your only option is to continue pointlessly or start over from level 0.  The crafting system has 25 recipes, and is a huge sink of time and resources.  Everything is geared around "numbers go up".  Every time you warp to a new level, there is always an ambush by a huge mob of pirates, sometimes assisted by the mob of pirates waiting to ambush the warp-gate positioned nearby.

There is no replay value.  There isn't even any value in finishing one play-through.  I am uninstalling and hiding the title in my library, so I don't forget and accidentally give it another try.

Casual, fun, laid-back space mining game.  With the occasional pirate attack. It's a very old game, but I like it. 
There is, however, [b]A HUGE ISSUE WITH MODERN HD SCREEN RESOLUTIONS MAKING THE TEXT AND UI WINDOWS & BUTTONS APPEAR MICROSCOPIC[/b]  BUT I HAVE FIXED IT.  [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3033353871]Click here to read my guide if you encounter the same problem when you play the game.[/url]

Now I'll tell you some specifics about the game.
You can setup various options when you start a new game;
galaxy size (number of star systems), amount of starting money, ship you start with, death penalties or perma-death, number and frequency of pirate squads, how quickly jobs expire and refresh, likelihood of finding more advanced asteroids in each system, your face portrait, your name, and - this is IMPORTANT - what condition you want to set for "VICTORY".  You can set it to end the game when you earn a certain number of credits, or when you murder the pirate officer in every star system, or a couple other options.  

You can also MOD THE GAME YOURSELF using the txt files in the "MOD_DATA" folder if you feel like it's lacking something.  

There are only 32 ships in the game that you can buy and fly, but each one is built differently.  
You will travel between star systems.  Land at space stations to sell merchandise, buy ship upgrades, buy skill upgrades, modify your equipment, buy/swap ships, or turn in job orders for extra money.  Then you go out to complete various simple jobs.  Like "transfer 1200 food to station X" so you buy 1200 food items and truck them over to the correct station to turn in the job there.  Or you can go mine asteroids for minerals and profits.  The minerals can be used to upgrade the equipment on your ship; the raw asteroid ore can be sold for money.  Or you can go bounty hunting and murder some pirates.  
Your ship has several numbers you need to keep track of.  Energy lets you use your systems (like your laser guns, mining lasers, shield boosters, and afterburners).  Fuel lets you travel from place to place; if you run out then your engine drains your energy instead.  Run out of both and you're stuck until your energy recharges.  Hull is your HP basically; if you get damaged you need to return to a station and pay to have it fixed, if it drops to zero then you die.  Shields soak up damage before your hull does, they will recharge slowly over time or automatically at a station.  And your cargo limit determines how much stuff you can carry.  Then later on, in some of the bigger ships you also will be able to carry and launch drones to help you fight pirates or mine asteroids.  Just remember to recall your drones before you try to land on a station!!

The story is, you got arrested for "bad thoughts about The Corporation" so they're forcing you to work off your fines as an asteroid miner on the edge of civilized space.  ...  Whatever "victory condition" you set determines how you end up paying off your fine or escaping this space prison colony or whatever.  Thats' it.  You're basically free to do as you please after you finish the tutorial, assuming you even bother to follow the tutorial.

Finally got around to playing this one, and it's kinda underwhelming. It's a weird mix of a bunch of conflicting mechanics. None of them are bad individually, but the mixture doesn't help any of them. It's a arcadey space combat game with manual control of your ship, but your weapons are auto-target only and you can actually just auto-play the combat from a zoomed out perspective. It's a game where money is used as a leveling mechanic in that you can buy bigger ships and better gear for those ships, but you also have an XP system which feeds a level which earns a skill point which is only used to buy (with money and skill points) passive upgrades to your pilot. Neither of these are bad systems, but having two currencies seems unnecessarily limiting in this case.
I played the game for nearly 20 hours, but a majority of that time is just clearing out all the asteroids and selling them in a system after destroying all the random pirate enemies that were slightly harder than the last one. I eventually died, because I pushed the combat a bit too far and blew up, and just kinda haven't had the urge to see if there's anything at the end if I managed to go through those last few systems.

Not sure I'd buy this game anymore, but it was probably pretty decent at the time of it's release.

I think its because all the jobs just exist, rather than you accepting quests.  Being able to have a list of the jobs I'm working on tucked off to the side would've been a HUGE help for me!

There is no storyline here, really.  The music is a LOT louder than the weapon noises...I had to turn the music volume way down so I could hear when I was being shot at (in case I looked away from the screen).  But then the noises of the menus when docked were loud...I wish there had been more settings here.

Everything else you know and love is there.  Drones, shields, beam/bullet/missile weapons.  There was a surprisingly large variety of ships, weapons, and mods available.  In fact, I wish the "Garage" had options to sort the weapons, mining lasers, and whatnot by type so that outfitting my ship was easier.

When you start the game, you have the option to select a lot of your settings.  For example, by default killing the pirate officer in a system causes pirates to stop respawning.  I like this, but maybe you don't?  Just change that setting!  Do you want asteroids to "regrow"?  How quickly should market prices change?  All of that is here!

When you complete a game by either reaching a specific dollar amount or clearing pirates from a certain amount of systems (your choice, that can be customized too), then you can restart with your same gear.

I'd love to see the minor changes I mentioned above happen, but it looks like the developer is working on a sequel type game.  No worries!  I'm not 100% sure this game is worth the current normal price of $10, but even at half off I think it'd be a good buy.

No es sencillo clasificarlo, porque aunque tiene elementos de un RPG como la subida de nivel y la mejora de equipo, hay otras tantas peculiaridades características que no tiene. Las galaxias se crean de manera procedural, pero su tamaño de serie parece ser bastante pequeño por lo que es recomendable aumentarlo un poco. Relacionado con esto último, con las opciones por defecto, resulta muy difícil llegar a manejar las naves de nivel más alto (hay una más que respetable colección de ellas) porque se alcanza el final demasiado rápido. Es cierto que el juego da la opción de comenzar una galaxia nueva desde el principio conservando la nave, pero personalmente no tenía demasiados alicientes para hacer casi todo de nuevo. 

La premisa de la historia es interesante, una especie de recluso espacial que ha de ganarse su libertad pagando la deuda mediante la minería. En realidad también tenemos la opción del comercio y el combate contra piratas para conseguir créditos, aunque al final es inevitable picar rocas. No obstante esta historia no se desarrolla apenas, y el juego se centra sobre todo en el plano jugable. A nivel de manejo me recuerda un poco a EvE Online, pero con diferencias enormes claro está. Tendremos que ir pasando de sistema eliminando a los "jefes" pirata, y eso nos obligará a tener ciertas habilidades de combate (o minar como si no hubiera un mañana para poder comprar el mejor equipo posible). Click where you want to go.  You can steer but it's not the way to play.  I don't think my controller will work either, but again, this isn't a flight sim.  I find it relaxing and fun at least having just started playing.

Also, this game has been called "Eve Light".  I played a fair amount of Eve a long time ago, and tried it out a while ago - but you know how that's going to go.  Like all other MMORPGs - Eve's not for everyone.  I'm pretty happy to find there's something at least claiming to be an alternative, even if it can't possibly be as huge as Eve is.

The game is unthinkably easy - at least if you build a universe using the default settings.  It's really just a clicker with a space ship attached to it.  You have to work very very hard to make it challenging - and I'm not even sure if it's possible.  Why?  I suppose if you never bought any upgrades it might start to faintly resemble something almost difficult - but with upgrades, and if you buy the biggest ship you can afford at all times, you'll be smothering the little ant pirates that you encounter - and you can see from a mile away what HP and how powerful the pirate ships are, so it's easy to figure out whether to try to kill them, or just mine for a while.

The game can be made arbitrarily more difficult.  That will increase the play-time a lot, as it will take much longer to reach all the content.  I recommend upping the difficulty (at least to 130% or so) to get an idea how you like it - I'm playing at 167% difficulty, and dying occasionally - which feels about right.

It's a relaxing little game and one that allows a modest amount of time to be sunk into it as my playtime will attest to. As a former EVE Online addict/player I was itching for a return to the space combat/trade genre without the MMORPG aspect that had consumed my life. Astrox had been billed as a sort of Eve-lite, so it was worth a go.

There are many similarities, but the depth of ship customisation, universe size etc. is much smaller. And that's a good thing because it meant I actually managed to complete the game before the whole experience descended into a futile never-ending grind. At least in EVE Online the grinding feels like you are working your way up a food chain. In Astrox it's just a speed hump on the way to the next system.

It was worth the time I spent on it but if you really want a large in-depth living universe then EVE Online, and not this, is what you are really after.
This is a great game to relax and lose a few more hours than you intended to.
